#### Comparing multiple proportions: The Marascuilo procedure {#sec-prc-474}

[**Testing for equal proportions of defects**]{#sec-prc-474-testing-equal}

[Earlier](#sec-prc-46), we discussed how to test whether several populations have the same proportion of defects. The example given there led to rejection of the null hypothesis of equality.

[**Marascuilo procedure allows comparison of all possible pairs of proportions**]{#sec-prc-474-allows-comparison}

Rejecting the null hypothesis only allows us to conclude that not (in this case) all lots are equal with respect to the proportion of defectives. However, it does not tell us which lot or lots caused the rejection.

The Marascuilo procedure enables us to simultaneously test the differences of all pairs of proportions when there are several populations under investigation.

**The Marascuilo Procedure**

[**Step 1: compute differences $p_i - p_j$**]{#sec-prc-474-step1}

Assume we have samples of size $n_i$ ($i = 1, \, 2, \, \ldots, \, k$) from $k$ populations. The first step of this procedure is to compute the differences $p_i - p_j$, (where $i$ is not equal to $j$) among all $k(k-1)/2$ pairs of proportions.

The absolute values of these differences are the test-statistics.

[**Step 2: compute test statistics**]{#sec-prc-474-step2}

Step 2 is to pick a significance level and compute the corresponding critical values for the Marascuilo procedure from

$$ r_{ij} = \sqrt{\chi^2_{1-\alpha, \, k-1}} \,\, \sqrt{\frac{p_i(1-p_i)}{n_i} + \frac{p_j(1-p_j)}{n_j}} \, . $$

[**Step 3: compare test statistics against corresponding critical values**]{#sec-prc-474-step3}

The third and last step is to compare each of the $k(k-1)/2$ test statistics against its corresponding critical $r_{ij}$ value. Those pairs that have a test statistic that exceeds the critical value are significant at the $\alpha$ level.

**Example**

[**Sample proportions**]{#sec-prc-474-sample-proportions}

To illustrate the Marascuilo procedure, we use the data from the previous [example](#sec-prc-46-data). Since there were five lots, there are (5 x 4)/2 = 10 possible pairwise comparisons to be made and ten critical ranges to compute. The five sample proportions are:

```{r}
#| label: verify-prc-474-proportions
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

nonconforming <- c(36, 46, 42, 63, 38)
n_i <- rep(300, 5)
p <- nonconforming / n_i

tibble(Lot = 1:5, `$p_i$` = p) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, align = "lr")
```

$$ \begin{aligned}
p_1 &= 36/300 = 0.120 \\
p_2 &= 46/300 = 0.153 \\
p_3 &= 42/300 = 0.140 \\
p_4 &= 63/300 = 0.210 \\
p_5 &= 38/300 = 0.127 \\
\end{aligned} $$

[**Table of critical values**]{#sec-prc-474-critical-values}

For an overall level of significance of 0.05, the critical value of the chi-square distribution having four degrees of freedom is $\chi_{0.95, \, 4}^2$ = 9.488 and the square root of 9.488 is 3.080. Calculating the 10 absolute differences and the 10 critical values leads to the following summary table.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prc-474-marascuilo
#| tbl-cap: "Marascuilo pairwise comparisons of lot proportions"
#| code-fold: true
k <- length(p)
chi2_crit <- qchisq(0.95, k - 1)
sqrt_chi2_crit <- sqrt(chi2_crit)

pairs <- combn(k, 2)
value <- apply(pairs, 2, \(ij) abs(p[ij[1]] - p[ij[2]]))
critical_range <- apply(pairs, 2, \(ij) sqrt_chi2_crit * sqrt(p[ij[1]] * (1 - p[ij[1]]) / n_i[ij[1]] + p[ij[2]] * (1 - p[ij[2]]) / n_i[ij[2]]))

tibble(
  Contrast = paste0("$\\lvert p_", pairs[1, ], " - p_", pairs[2, ], " \\rvert$"),
  Value = value,
  `Critical range` = critical_range,
  Significant = ifelse(value > critical_range, "yes", "no")
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, align = "lrrl")
```

The table of critical values can be generated using both Dataplot code and R code; see the companion R script for this section.

[**No individual contrast is statistically significant**]{#sec-prc-474-conclusions}

A difference is statistically significant if its value exceeds the critical range value. In this example, even though the null hypothesis of equality was [rejected](#sec-prc-46-conclusions) earlier, there is not enough data to conclude any particular difference is significant. Note, however, that all the comparisons involving population 4 come the closest to significance - leading us to suspect that more data might actually show that population 4 does have a significantly higher proportion of defects.
